newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. sanctions body to take up flights by Gaddafi.
newsitem.headline: U.N. sanctions body to take up flights by Gaddafi.

text.p: American U.N. envoy Bill Richardson said on Tuesday Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi had been on a "joy ride" aimed at defying U.N. sanctions and the issue would be taken up by the Security Council's sanctions committee.
He was referring to a flight last week by a flotilla of four Libyan aircraft that took Gaddafi and others to Niger and Nigeria, despite a U.N. air embargo against Libya over the Lockerbie affair.
The Libyan news agency said Gaddafi was visiting the West African countries to hold prayers marking the Moslem new year as head of the Islamic Popular Leadership, an organisation he created in 1989.
"I raised the Libyan issue," Richardson told reporters after closed-door council consultations on a number of issues.

"We are very concerned about these sanctions violations. The Libyan matter has been referred to the sanctions committee. It is obvious Mr. Gaddafi is in a joy ride trying to defy the council. Our hope is that the council and the sanctions committee will deal with this issue very soon."
Council president Park Soo Gil of South Korea said there was agreement among council members to refer the matter to the sanctions committee, which has the same membership as the 15-nation council.
The committee would meet either Thursday or Friday and seek explanations "by the three countries concerned" -- Libya, Niger and Nigeria -- and establish the facts.

In Washington, U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns was asked about the involvement of the two West African countries which, under the sanctions rules, should have denied landing rights to Libyan planes and impounded any that landed.

"Not only was there complicity, there was direct involvement," he said. "The president of Niger flew on the Libyan plane with Gaddafi between Niamey and Lagos. And then there was a hero's welcome for Gaddafi by the dictators in Lagos. So there's no question in our minds what's happening."
Burns noted the United States already had "a difficult relationship" with Nigeria as "a major violator of human rights."
"And we didn't have a great relationship with Niger, and now that relationship's gotten a lot worse," he added.

Libya has been the target since 1992 of a ban on all international flights, an arms embargo and the downgrading of diplomatic relations for failing to extradite two men wanted by Britain and the United States in the 1988 mid-air bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270 people.
The sanctions, which were later extended, also penalise Libya for failing to cooperate in an investigation into the 1989 bombing of a French UTA airliner over Niger that killed 171 people.
The Security Council issued a statement last month rapping Libya for flying pilgrims from Libya to Saudi Arabia in breach of sanctions.
A statement read at a brief council meeting April 4 said "this clear violation" was "totally unacceptable" and called on Libya to "refrain from any further such violations."

It was the third consecutive year Libya had violated sanctions by flying pilgrims to Jeddah on an unauthorised flight even though the council had given permission for an Egyptian airline to ferry Libyans wishing to make the annual pilgrimage to Mecca.
Tripoli has said in the past that pilgrims do not need U.N. authorisation to perform their religious duties.
Libya also violated sanctions in January by flying an official delegation to Accra, Ghana, and back. In June 1996 a Libyan-registered plane flew Gaddafi to Cairo for an Arab summit meeting.

Libya, backed by the Arab League, the Organisation of African Unity and the non-aligned movement, has offered to allow the two men wanted in the Lockerbie case to stand trial before a Scottish judge under Scottish law at the seat of the World Court at The Hague. Britain and the United States have rejected this as unacceptable.
